mainTopic: The כהן's belt, and what counts as extra garments or a barrier (חציצה) between a כהן's body and his priestly garments, including תפילין
overview: The amud opens by finishing the previous discussion: the כהנים wore the אבנט at elbow height. רב אשי then tells how a Persian king straightened הונא בר נתן's belt because the Jews are 'a kingdom of כהנים', and אמימר calls this a fulfillment of ישעיהו's promise. Next the גמרא quotes a משנה from עירובין: a כהן with a hurt finger may wrap it with a reed in the מקדש on שבת. רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא and רבי יוחנן argue over whether a small cloth wrap is allowed, given in two versions: one about יתור בגדים (extra garments) and one about חציצה (a barrier), with רבא's rule in the name of רב חסדא about a three-by-three size. The גמרא then lists many questions about what blocks the garment from being 'on his flesh': wind, a louse, fine dust, the armpit, his own hand, a dangling thread and his hair. רבי זירא asks whether תפילין block, and רבי אמי answers from a settled tradition that they do. After challenges from ברייתות, the גמרא concludes that hand תפילין block and head תפילין do not. It begins explaining why the head is different, and that explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The belt is worn at elbow level
steps.stepSummary: The previous discussion ends: the כהנים wore their אבנט at the height of their elbows.
steps.simpleTranslation: [They wore the belt] at the level of their elbows.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last words of a statement that started on the previous page. It tells us where the כהנים tied the אבנט: at the level of their elbows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion was asking exactly where on the body the אבנט is tied. This line gives the answer: not low at the waist and not up at the chest, but at elbow level.

keyTerms.meaning: The belt or sash, one of the priestly garments

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new topic. It finishes a sentence that began on the previous page about where the אבנט sits.

phrases.english: At the level of their elbows.
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from the previous page. 'They' are the כהנים tying their belt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the statement from the previous daf about where the אבנט is placed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The אבנט of the כהנים is worn at elbow level.

steps.title: A Persian king fixes a Jew's belt
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reports that הונא בר נתן told him how King איזגדר lowered his raised belt and quoted 'a kingdom of כהנים and a holy nation'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: הונא בר נתן told me: Once I was standing before King איזגדר, and my belt was pulled up too high. He pulled it down into place and said to me: 'A kingdom of כהנים and a holy nation' is written about you.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the topic is where the belt should sit, the גמרא tells a story about a belt worn too high. A non-Jewish king fixed it himself and said Jews should look dignified like כהנים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story connects to the belt discussion: a belt has a proper, dignified place. The king saw all of the Jewish people as a 'kingdom of כהנים', so he expected a Jew's clothing to be neat and properly placed.

keyTerms.meaning: A kingdom of כהנים (from the פסוק about the Jewish people)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי, אָמַר לִי הוּנָא בַּר נָתָן:
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said: Huna bar Natan said to me:
Once I was standing
before Izgadar the king,
and my belt was raised up too high,
and he brought it down into place,
phrases.notes: The king himself reached over and pulled the belt down to where it belongs.

phrases.english: and he said to me:
"A kingdom of priests and a holy nation" is written about you.
phrases.notes: שמות 19:6

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי, אָמַר לִי הוּנָא בַּר נָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells a related story about a belt worn in the wrong place, linked to the elbow-height rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Jews, called a 'kingdom of כהנים', should wear their belts properly and look dignified.

steps.title: אמימר: kings shall serve you
steps.stepSummary: When הונא בר נתן told אמימר the story, אמימר said the פסוק 'kings shall be your caretakers' came true for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: When I came before אמימר, he said to me: The פסוק 'And kings shall be your caretakers' was fulfilled in you.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. אמימר comments that a king fixing a Jew's clothing fulfills a נבואה from ישעיהו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק promises that kings will one day care for the Jewish people. A king personally fixing a Jew's belt was a small taste of that promise, so אמימר saw it as a fulfillment.
steps.whatToRemember: The story about the belt shows that the clothing of the Jewish people, a 'kingdom of כהנים', deserves dignity. אמימר sees a king's care for that dignity as a fulfillment of ישעיהו's promise.

phrases.english: When I came before Ameimar,
phrases.notes: The 'I' is still הונא בר נתן, telling אמימר what happened with the king.

phrases.english: he said to me: It has been fulfilled in you:
"And kings shall be your caretakers."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 49:23

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story with אמימר's comment on what happened.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A king serving a Jew fulfills the פסוק 'kings shall be your caretakers'.

steps.title: A כהן with an injured finger
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה in עירובין: a כהן may wrap a reed on an injured finger in the מקדש on שבת, but not outside it. Drawing blood out is forbidden everywhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned there: A כהן who hurt his finger may wrap a reed around it in the מקדש, but not in the rest of the country. But if he wants to squeeze blood out of it, it is forbidden both here and there.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic about the priestly garments by quoting a משנה from somewhere else. This sets up the next steps, which discuss what kind of wrapping is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wrapping a reed on a wound is a kind of healing, which the רבנן forbade on שבת. In the מקדש this rabbinic rule is relaxed so the כהן can do the service, but outside the מקדש it stays. Squeezing out blood is a more serious act, so it is forbidden even in the מקדש.

keyTerms.meaning: The rest of the country, outside the מקדש
Here and there, in both places

steps.confusionAlert: This משנה is about שבת. That is why wrapping is allowed in the מקדש but not outside it.

phrases.english: We learned there:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in מסכת עירובין.

phrases.english: A priest who was injured on his finger
may wrap a reed around it in the Temple,
but not in the rest of the country.
And if it is to draw blood out of it,
here and there it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the belt story to a new topic about the priestly garments: a bandage on a כהן's finger.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כהן may wrap a reed on an injured finger in the מקדש on שבת but not outside it. Drawing blood is forbidden in both places.

steps.title: Only a reed, not a cloth bandage
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא says the משנה allowed only a reed. A small cloth wrap would count as יתור בגדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה son of רבי חייא said: They only taught this about a reed. But a small cloth strip counts as extra garments.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא limits the משנה. Only a reed is allowed, because a piece of cloth would be like adding an extra garment to the כהן's clothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A כהן must serve in exactly the garments the תורה lists, no more and no less. A reed is not a garment, but a small cloth band is fabric, so it counts as adding to the clothing. That is why רבי יהודה says the משנה only allowed a reed.

keyTerms.meaning: A small strip of cloth or band
Extra garments, wearing more than the required priestly garments

steps.whyThisMatters: This brings in the rule of יתור בגדים, the first of two reasons (the other is חציצה) the coming discussion uses to judge a bandage on a כהן's finger.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Chiyya, said:
They taught this only about a reed,
but a small cloth strip
is extra garments.
phrases.notes: He means it counts as adding to the priestly clothing, which is not allowed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the משנה to a reed only, leaving out a cloth bandage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A cloth bandage on a כהן's finger counts as יתור בגדים, so only a reed is allowed.

steps.title: Extra garments only where garments are worn
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says יתור בגדים applies only where the priestly garments are worn. A cloth on the finger is not extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: They only said 'extra garments' about the places where garments are worn. But in a place where no garments are worn, it is not extra.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן disagrees with רבי יהודה. He says a cloth on the finger is fine, because the hands are not covered by any of the priestly garments.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two argue about what counts as 'extra'. For רבי יהודה, any cloth is extra. For רבי יוחנן, it is only extra if it is added on a part of the body that the priestly garments cover. Since the finger is uncovered, a cloth there does not add to the garments.

keyTerms.meaning: They did not say (the rule) except...
In a place where the garments are worn

steps.whatToRemember: The argument: רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא says any cloth bandage is יתור בגדים. רבי יוחנן says it is only יתור בגדים on a part of the body covered by the priestly garments, so a finger bandage is fine.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
They did not speak of extra garments
except in a place where garments are worn,
but in a place where garments are not worn,
it is not extra.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: לֹא אָמְרוּ יִתּוּר בְּגָדִים אֶלָּא בִּמְקוֹם בְּגָדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא and limits יתור בגדים to the places the garments cover.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: יתור בגדים applies only where priestly garments are worn, so a cloth on the finger is permitted.

steps.title: Why not forbid the cloth because it blocks the hand?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: even if the cloth is not an extra garment, it should still be forbidden because it is a חציצה between the hand and the vessel.
steps.simpleTranslation: But he should get the rule that it is forbidden because it is a barrier!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's permission to wrap a cloth on the finger. Even if it is not יתור בגדים, a wrapped finger seems to block the hand from touching the holy vessel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן only addressed one possible problem, extra garments. The גמרא points to a second possible problem: a barrier between the כהן's hand and the vessel makes the service invalid. If so, the cloth should be forbidden anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him get the rule from (a different reason)
A barrier between the כהן's body and the vessel or the service

phrases.english: But let him derive it because of a barrier!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's leniency from step 6 using a different prohibition.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that a cloth on the finger is permitted
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even if it is not an extra garment, a wrap on the serving hand should be a חציצה and invalidate the service.

steps.title: The wound is on the left hand or off the serving spot
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יוחנן means a wound on the left hand, or a spot on the right hand that is not used for the service.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is on the left hand. Or else, it is not in the place used for the service.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the case. The cloth is in a place where it does not get in the way of the service, so there is no חציצה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חציצה is only a problem where the hand actually does the service. The service is done with the right hand, so a wrap on the left hand blocks nothing. A second answer: even on the right hand, the wrap can sit on a part of the hand that does not touch the vessel.

keyTerms.meaning: The part of the body used for the service

phrases.english: On the left hand.
phrases.notes: The service is done with the right hand, so a wrap on the left hand blocks nothing.

phrases.english: Alternatively, not in the place of the service.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׂמֹאל. אִי נָמֵי, שֶׁלֹּא בִּמְקוֹם עֲבוֹדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 7 by limiting the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The cloth is on the hand that does the service and blocks contact with the vessel.
steps.terutzMaskana: The cloth is on the left hand, or on a non-serving part of the right hand, so there is no חציצה.

steps.title: רבא's rule: one thread on the garments, 3×3 elsewhere
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רבי יוחנן argues with רבא, who quotes רב חסדא: where garments are worn even one thread is a barrier, and elsewhere only a 3×3 piece counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this argues with רבא. For רבא said in the name of רב חסדא: In a place where the garments are worn, even one thread is a barrier. In a place where the garments are not worn, a piece three by three is a barrier, and anything smaller is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different opinion, from רבא quoting רב חסדא, and points out that it does not fit with רבי יוחנן. This sets up the comparison in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said nothing outside the garment area counts as extra. רבא says that even outside the garment area, a cloth of 3×3 fingerbreadths does count. So the two disagree about a larger cloth worn where the garments are not.

keyTerms.meaning: Three by three (fingerbreadths), the minimum size of a meaningful cloth

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets two size rules, one for where the garments are worn and one for elsewhere, which the next steps measure against the earlier opinions.

phrases.english: And it argues with רבא,
phrases.notes: "It" is רבי יוחנן's ruling from step 6.

phrases.english: for רבא said in the name of רב חסדא:
In a place of the garments,
even one thread is a barrier.
Not in a place of the garments,
three by three are a barrier,
phrases.notes: Three fingerbreadths by three fingerbreadths of cloth.

phrases.english: less than this is not a barrier.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפְלִיגָא דְּרָבָא דְּאָמַר רָבָא אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that רבי יוחנן's ruling (step 6) conflicts with a known rule of רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Where garments are worn, even one thread is a barrier. Elsewhere, only a piece of 3×3 fingerbreadths or more is a barrier.

steps.title: Does רבא also argue with רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says רבא clearly argues with רבי יוחנן, and asks whether he also argues with רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא.
steps.simpleTranslation: With רבי יוחנן he certainly argues. With רבי יהודה son of רבי חייא, shall we say that he argues?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks how far the disagreement goes. It sets up a question about whether רבא's 3×3 rule clashes with רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא said even a tiny cloth wrap on the finger counts as an extra garment (step 5). רבא says that outside the garment area, a piece smaller than 3×3 does not count. A small finger wrap is smaller than 3×3, so it looks like רבא disagrees with him too.

phrases.english: With רבי יוחנן, he certainly argues;
with רבי יהודה son of רבי חייא,
shall we say that he argues?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רבא's rule from step 9 and compares it with the opinion in step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does רבא's 3×3 minimum contradict רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא, who forbids even a small finger wrap?

steps.title: A small finger wrap is different because it is important
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a small finger wrap is considered important, so even רבא would count it as a garment.
steps.simpleTranslation: A small wrap is different, because it is considered important.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבא does not argue with רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא. A finger wrap is a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's 3×3 minimum applies to an ordinary scrap of cloth. A wrap made to fit a finger is a real piece of clothing for that spot, so it counts even though it is smaller. רבא's rule therefore stands, and the finger wrap is an exception to it.

keyTerms.meaning: A small strip or wrap of cloth

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן: nothing outside the garment area counts as extra. רבא: outside it, only 3×3 counts. רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא can agree with רבא, because a small finger wrap is important and counts as a garment.

phrases.english: A small wrap is different, because it is significant.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 10.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No disagreement: a small finger wrap is important and counts as a garment even under 3×3, so רבא agrees with רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא.

steps.title: Second version: רבי יהודה says only a reed is allowed
steps.stepSummary: In the second version, רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא limits the leniency to a reed. A small sash is a barrier.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some tell the story another way. רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא said: the rule allowing a wrap applies only to a reed, but a small sash is a barrier.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a second version of the argument about wrapping a wounded finger. רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא still allows only a reed, but now his reason is that a small sash is a barrier (חציצה).
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both versions רבי יהודה allows only a reed. What changes is his reason: in the first version a small sash was forbidden as יתור בגדים (extra garments). Here it is forbidden because it is a barrier (חציצה).

keyTerms.meaning: Another version: a different way of reporting the same discussion
They only taught this about: a phrase that limits a rule
A small sash, a little strip of cloth
It is a barrier; it blocks contact

steps.confusionAlert: This is a second version of the same argument, not a new topic. Do not mix up what each אמורא says here with what he said in the first version.

phrases.english: Some say it in another version:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Chiya, said:
They taught this only about a reed,
phrases.notes: The rule in the משנה that a כהן may wrap a wounded finger with a reed.

phrases.english: but a small sash is a barrier.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of the dispute that the earlier steps analyzed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a reed may be wrapped on the finger; a small sash is a חציצה.

steps.title: Second version: רבי יוחנן's size rule matches רב חסדא
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that where garments are worn, even something smaller than 3×3 is a barrier. Where garments are not worn, only a 3×3 piece is a barrier. This is the same as רבא's quote from רב חסדא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: they said something smaller than 3×3 is a barrier only where garments are worn. Where garments are not worn, a 3×3 piece is a barrier and anything smaller is not. This is the same as what רבא said in the name of רב חסדא.
steps.whatsHappening: In the second version, רבי יוחנן gives a rule based on where the cloth is on the body. The גמרא notes that this now matches רבא quoting רב חסדא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first version said רבי יוחנן argues with רבא. In this version they agree. Where the בגדי כהונה are worn, any small piece is a barrier. On other parts of the body, only a 3×3 piece blocks.

keyTerms.meaning: Three by three fingerbreadths, the minimum size of cloth that counts
The part of the body where the priestly garments are worn
And this is the same as

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the main difference between the two versions. Here רבי יוחנן and רבא agree, so the next question is whether they argue with רבי יהודה instead.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא אָמְרוּ חֲצִיצָה בְּפָחוֹת מִשָּׁלֹשׁ עַל שָׁלֹשׁ –
phrases.english: They did not say that less than three by three is a barrier
except in the place where the garments are worn,
but in a place where the garments are not worn,
three by three is a barrier,
less than that is not a barrier.
And this is what Rava said in the name of Rav Chisda.
phrases.notes: This is the rule from step 9. In this version, רבי יוחנן and רבא say the same thing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the second version by giving רבי יוחנן's side.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Where garments are worn, any size is a barrier. Elsewhere, only 3×3 is a barrier.

steps.title: Does this argue with רבי יהודה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבא (now the same as רבי יוחנן) argues with רבי יהודה, who said a small sash is a barrier.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this argues with רבי יהודה בריה דרבי חייא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests there may be an argument. רבא says a small piece on the finger is not a barrier, but רבי יהודה says a small sash is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The finger is not where garments are worn, so by רבא's rule a sash smaller than 3×3 should not block. רבי יהודה says even a small sash does block. So it looks like they disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? It introduces a suggested conclusion

phrases.english: Shall we say it argues
with Rabbi Yehuda, son of Rabbi Chiya?

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא פְּלִיגָא אַדְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two statements of the second version.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Are רבא's size rule and רבי יהודה's small-sash rule in conflict?

steps.title: A small sash is important
steps.stepSummary: There is no argument. A small sash is important, so it counts as a garment even though it is small.
steps.simpleTranslation: A small sash is different, because it is considered important.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two opinions do not argue. A small sash is a special case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's 3×3 rule is about ordinary scraps of cloth. A sash is a real, important item, so it counts as a garment even below that size. That is why רבי יהודה calls it a barrier.

phrases.english: A small sash is different, because it is important.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question by treating a small sash as an exception.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No argument, because a small sash is important and counts as a garment.

steps.title: Why did the משנה choose a reed?
steps.stepSummary: According to רבי יוחנן, a small sash on the finger is not a barrier. So why did the משנה mention a reed instead of the bigger new idea of a small sash?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי יוחנן, why mention a reed specifically? Let it teach us about a small sash!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's view. It asks about the משנה's choice of example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If even an important small sash is not a barrier on the finger, the משנה should have used that example. It would teach more than a reed does. Choosing the weaker example needs an explanation.

phrases.english: And according to Rabbi Yochanan, why specifically a reed?
Let it teach us about a small sash!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the comparison to a challenge about the wording of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's choice of a reed, according to רבי יוחנן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה should teach the bigger new idea. A small sash being allowed would be a bigger new idea than a reed.

steps.title: The משנה teaches that a reed heals
steps.stepSummary: The משנה chose a reed to teach, in passing, a side fact: a reed has healing power.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us something along the way: that a reed heals.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The משנה picked a reed on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Mentioning a reed teaches a bonus fact: a reed helps a wound heal. That is a good reason to use the reed example, even though a sash would teach more about barriers.

keyTerms.meaning: Something taught in passing, along the way

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's size rule need not clash with רבי יהודה, because a small sash is important. And even for רבי יוחנן, who would allow a small sash, the משנה mentions a reed to teach in passing that a reed heals.

phrases.aramaic: מִילְּתָא אַגַּב אוֹרְחֵיהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן,
phrases.english: It teaches us something in passing,
that a reed heals.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִילְּתָא אַגַּב אוֹרְחֵיהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about the משנה's wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why the משנה chose its example
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the reed example was a weaker lesson for no reason.
steps.terutzMaskana: The reed was chosen to teach, in passing, that a reed heals.

steps.title: What if wind lifts the garment off his body?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks about wind getting into a כהן's garment and lifting it off his skin. Is that still 'on his flesh,' or is it just the normal way clothes are worn?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: if wind got into his garment, what is the law? Do we need the garment 'on his flesh,' which it is not right now? Or perhaps this is simply the normal way clothes are worn?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question from רבא about the priestly garments. It sets out two sides, and no answer is given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the garment must be 'on his flesh.' If wind lifts it, it is not touching his body. But clothes always move this way when worn, so maybe it still counts as properly worn.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked; he raised a question of doubt
On his flesh, the פסוק's requirement for the garments
The normal way of wearing clothes

phrases.english: Rava asked:
If wind got into his garment, what is the law?
Do we need it to be 'on his flesh,'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 6:3

phrases.english: and here that is missing;
or perhaps this is the normal way of wearing clothes?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רָבָא נִכְנְסָה לוֹ רוּחַ בְּבִגְדוֹ מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from barriers between the body and the vessel to whether a lifted garment still counts as 'on his flesh.'
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a garment lifted by wind still count as 'on his flesh,' or is it invalid because it is not touching his body?

steps.title: Does a louse under the garment count as a barrier?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא continues its list of questions and asks whether a louse between the כהן's body and his garment is a חציצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A louse: does it block (between the garment and the body)?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another question to the list: if a louse is under the כהן's garment, does it count as a barrier between the garment and his skin? This opens the question, and the next step will make it sharper.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The garments must be 'on his flesh' with nothing separating them from the body. A louse is a small creature sitting right on the skin, so it is not clear whether it counts as 'something in between.'

keyTerms.meaning: A louse (a small bug that lives on the body).
What is the law? (opens a question)
That it blocks / a barrier between the body and the garment.

phrases.english: A louse: what is the law, does it block?
phrases.notes: He means: does it block between the כהן's garment and his skin?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another question in the same list as the wind question of step 18, all about what separates the garment from the body.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a louse between the garment and the skin counts as a barrier.

steps.title: The question is only about a live louse
steps.stepSummary: A dead louse is clearly a barrier. The real question is a live one: is it like part of the body because it keeps moving, or a barrier because the כהן is bothered by it?
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't ask about a dead louse, because it surely blocks. What about a live one? Do we say that since it comes and goes, it is like a growth and does not block? Or maybe, since he is bothered by it, it does block?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the question: a dead louse is obviously a barrier, so the question is only about a live louse. It then lays out the two sides of the doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: a live louse keeps moving around, so it is like a 'growth' on the body and not a separate object. Side two: the כהן is bothered by it and wants it gone. Something a person minds having on him counts as a barrier. The question is left open.

keyTerms.meaning: A growth: something treated as part of the body.
He is bothered by it / he minds it being there.
Or perhaps (introduces the other side of a question).

steps.confusionAlert: Being 'bothered' (קפידא) here is a reason for the louse TO be a barrier, not a reason against. Something a person minds having on his body is treated as a separate thing on him.

phrases.english: About a dead one, do not ask,
because it certainly blocks.
What about a live one?
Do we say: since it comes and goes,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets, and the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Both mean 'comes.'

phrases.english: it is a growth and does not block?
phrases.notes: 'Growth' means something treated like part of the body itself.

phrases.english: Or perhaps, since he is bothered by it,
it blocks?

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתָה לָא תִּבְּעֵי לָךְ, דְּוַדַּאי חָיְיצָא; חַיָּה מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the louse question of step 19 to a live louse and gives both sides of the doubt.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a live louse is treated as part of the body (because it moves) or as a barrier (because the כהן is bothered by it).

steps.title: Does dirt count as a barrier?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether dirt under the כהן's garment is a barrier.
steps.simpleTranslation: Dirt: does it block?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a new question: what about dirt between the garment and the body? It is setting up the next step, which will challenge this question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of question as the louse: does something on the skin separate the garment from the body?

phrases.english: Dirt: what is the law, does it block?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new question in the same list, moving from a louse to dirt.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether dirt between the garment and the skin counts as a barrier.

steps.title: Dirt is obviously a barrier
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: dirt surely blocks, so there is nothing to ask.
steps.simpleTranslation: Dirt certainly blocks!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own question: dirt is a real substance on the skin, so it is obviously a barrier. Why ask?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ordinary dirt is a clear separate layer between garment and body, so there is no reason to be unsure about it. This forces the question to be about something smaller.

phrases.english: Dirt certainly blocks!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the question just asked in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The question of whether dirt is a barrier (step 21).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Dirt is plainly a separate layer on the skin, so the answer is obvious and the question makes no sense.

steps.title: The real question is about fine dust
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא fixes the question: it is about a light layer of dust, not real dirt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what is the law about fine dust?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its objection by changing the case: the question was really about very fine dust, which is hardly noticeable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Real dirt surely blocks, but fine dust is so thin that maybe it doesn't count as a layer at all. The question stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (fixes or changes what was said before).
Fine dust, a very thin layer of dirt.

phrases.english: Rather, what is the law about fine dust?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection in step 22 by changing the case from dirt to fine dust.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the question was never about real dirt.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question seemed to be about ordinary dirt, which obviously blocks.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question is about fine dust, which may be too thin to count as a barrier. It stays unanswered.

steps.title: Does the gap at the armpit count as a barrier?
steps.stepSummary: At the armpit the garment does not touch the skin. Does that break the 'on his flesh' rule, or is it simply the normal way clothes are worn?
steps.simpleTranslation: The armpit: does it block? We need 'on his flesh,' and here it is not. Or perhaps this is the normal way of wearing clothes?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks one more question: at the armpit the garment hangs away from the skin. Does that count as a problem, or is it fine because that is how clothes are always worn?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: the פסוק requires the garment to be 'on his flesh,' and at the armpit it is not touching. Side two: every garment sits this way at the armpit, so this is normal wearing and not a real separation. This is like the wind question in step 18, and it is also left open.

keyTerms.meaning: 'On his flesh': the פסוק's requirement that the garment be on the body.
The normal way of wearing clothes.

steps.whatToRemember: All these questions test one idea: what breaks 'on his flesh'? A real object in between (dead louse, dirt) surely does. The open cases are things that may count as part of the body (live louse), are barely there (fine dust), or are just how clothes normally sit (armpit, wind).

phrases.english: The armpit: what is the law, does it block?
phrases.notes: He means the space where the garment hangs away from the skin under the arm.

phrases.english: We need 'on his flesh,'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 6:3

phrases.english: and here it is not there.
Or perhaps this is the way of wearing?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The last question in the list. It goes back to the reasoning of step 18 (normal way of wearing) and applies it to the armpit.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the gap at the armpit breaks the 'on his flesh' requirement, or is allowed because it is the normal way clothes are worn.

steps.title: His hand tucked inside his garment
steps.stepSummary: If the כהן puts his hand inside his garment against his chest, does his own hand count as a barrier?
steps.simpleTranslation: If the כהן put his hand inside the front of his garment, what is the law? Does his own body count as a barrier, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question. What if the thing between the garment and the skin is part of the כהן himself, his own hand?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the barriers were outside things like a louse or dust. Here the 'barrier' is his own body. The question is whether one part of his body can block another part from touching the garment.

keyTerms.meaning: His chest area, inside the front of his garment

phrases.english: If he put his hand into his bosom, what is the law?
Does his body block, or not?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another question in the same list of possible barriers, now about the כהן's own body.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Can the כהן's own body part count as a barrier between his garment and his skin?

steps.title: A thread under the garment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether a thread counts as a barrier.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about a thread: does it count as a barrier?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks about a thread caught between the garment and the skin. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A thread is a small, separate object. The question as first worded asks simply whether it blocks.

phrases.english: A thread: what is the law, does it block?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next question in the list.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a thread between the garment and the skin count as a barrier?

steps.title: A thread obviously blocks
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that a separate thread is surely a barrier, so there is nothing to ask.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a thread certainly blocks!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the question. A loose thread is clearly a barrier, so why ask?
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works just like the challenge about dirt in step 22. An obvious case cannot be the real question, so the question must be about something less clear.

phrases.english: A thread certainly blocks!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the question just asked.
steps.kashyaTarget: The question about a thread in step 26
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A separate thread is plainly a barrier, so the question has an obvious answer.

steps.title: The question is about a dangling thread
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא fixes the question: it is about a thread still hanging from the garment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, ask about a thread that is dangling from the garment: what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by changing the case. The thread is still attached to the garment but hanging loose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A thread still attached may count as part of the garment itself, so it would not block. But since it is about to fall off, maybe it already counts as a separate thing that blocks. That is the real doubt.

phrases.english: Rather, a dangling thread: what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question was about a loose, separate thread.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question is about a thread still attached but dangling. Is it part of the garment or a separate barrier?

steps.title: His hair inside his garment
steps.stepSummary: מר בר רב אשי asks whether the כהן's hair that gets between the garment and the skin is a barrier.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר בר רב אשי asked: if his hair came out into his garment, what is the law? Is his hair like his body, or not like his body?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question from מר בר רב אשי: the כהן's own hair slips under his garment and lies between it and his skin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If hair counts as part of his body, it is not a barrier. If hair is treated as something separate from the body, it would block the garment from the skin.

keyTerms.meaning: Asks a question he cannot settle

phrases.english: Mar bar Rav Ashi asked:
If his hair came out into his garment, what is the law?
Is his hair like his body,
or is it not like his body?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another body-related barrier question, similar to the hand question in step 25.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does hair count as part of the body, or as a separate thing that blocks?

steps.title: Do תפילין count as a barrier?
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא asks whether תפילין worn under the garment count as a barrier.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא asked: תפילין, do they count as a barrier?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא asks a new question about תפילין that the כהן wears under his garment. The גמרא will now explain exactly where the doubt lies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תפילין are a separate object, so you would expect them to block. But they are a מצוה worn on the body, which might make them different. The next steps sharpen this.

keyTerms.meaning: תפילין, the boxes worn on the arm and head

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira asked:
Tefillin: what is the law, do they block?

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַבִּי זֵירָא: תְּפִילִּין – מַהוּ שֶׁיָּחוֹצּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next question in the list of possible barriers.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do תפילין under the priestly garment count as a barrier?

steps.title: No question if night is not a time for תפילין
steps.stepSummary: According to the view that night is not a time for תפילין, they clearly block, both at night and by day.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who says night is not a time for תפילין, there is no question. Since they block at night, they also block by day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows רבי זירא's question. For one opinion the answer is obvious, so the question cannot be according to that opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If night is not a time for תפילין, wearing them at night is no מצוה, so they are just an object on the body and they block. And if they block at night, they are the same תפילין by day, so they block then too.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the one who says
Night is not a time for תפילין
Do not ask it; there is no question

phrases.english: According to the one who says
night is not a time for tefillin,
do not ask it;
since at night they block,
by day they also block.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלִּיבָּא דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר לַיְלָה לָאו זְמַן תְּפִילִּין הוּא – לָא תִּבְעֵי לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the question in step 30 by removing one opinion where the answer is clear.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: By the view that night is not a time for תפילין, they block both at night and by day, so there is no question by that view.

steps.title: The real question: does a מצוה on the body block?
steps.stepSummary: The question is only according to the view that night is a time for תפילין: does a מצוה worn on the body count as a barrier?
steps.simpleTranslation: When you ask, ask according to the one who says night is a time for תפילין. What is the law? Does a מצוה of the body block or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states רבי זירא's question in its sharp form. According to this view, תפילין are always a מצוה on the body, so maybe they are not a barrier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By this view there is never a time when wearing תפילין is not a מצוה. So the doubt is whether a מצוה that belongs to the body is treated like part of the body, or still as an outside object that blocks.

keyTerms.meaning: A מצוה of his body, worn on the body

steps.whatToRemember: The real question about תפילין only exists by the view that night is a time for תפילין. Then they are always a מצוה on the body, and the doubt is whether such a מצוה blocks.

phrases.english: When you ask it,
ask according to the one who says night is a time for tefillin;
what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: מִצְוָה דְגוּפֵיהּ – חָיֵיץ אוֹ לָא חָיֵיץ?
phrases.english: A מצוה of his body: does it block or not block?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ – לְמַאן דְּאָמַר לַיְלָה זְמַן תְּפִילִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After ruling out one view in step 31, the גמרא places the question in the other view and states the real doubt.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a מצוה worn on the body, like תפילין, count as a barrier between the כהן and his garments?

steps.title: רבי אמי: we have a clear tradition that תפילין block
steps.stepSummary: The question traveled until it reached רבי אמי, who answered from a fixed tradition that תפילין are a חציצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The question went around until it came to רבי אמי. He said: we have a settled teaching that תפילין do block.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא's open question from step 32 finally gets an answer. רבי אמי says there is a known tradition that תפילין block.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 32 asked whether a מצוה worn on the body could still count as a barrier. רבי אמי does not answer from logic. He quotes an established tradition: yes, even תפילין block between the כהן's body and his garments.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter rolled along, meaning the question was passed from one scholar to another
They block, meaning they count as a barrier (חציצה)

phrases.english: The matter rolled along,
and reached Rabbi Ami.
He said to him:
We have a settled teaching:
Tefillin block.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיגַּלְגַּל מִילְּתָא, וּמְטָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי אַמֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 32.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Do תפילין, a מצוה, count as a barrier under the כהן's garments?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. A settled tradition says תפילין block.

steps.title: A ברייתא suggests כהנים are only 'exempt' from תפילין
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says כהנים at their service are 'exempt' from תפילין. That wording seems to mean that if they did wear them, the תפילין would not block.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged him: כהנים at their service, לוים on their platform, and ישראלים at their watch are exempt from prayer and from תפילין. Doesn't this mean that if they put them on, the תפילין do not block?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי אמי's tradition with a ברייתא. The word 'exempt' suggests a כהן is allowed to wear תפילין, so they would not block.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Exempt' normally means 'you don't have to, but you may.' If a כהן may wear תפילין during the עבודה, they cannot be a חציצה, because that would make his service invalid. This clashes with רבי אמי.

keyTerms.meaning: The platform where the לוים sang in the בית המקדש
The watch of ישראלים who stood by while the daily קרבן was brought
Exempt, meaning not required but not forbidden

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
Kohanim at their service,
and Levites on their platform,
and Israelites at their watch,
are exempt from prayer and from tefillin.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי, לָאו אִם הִנִּיחָן אֵינָן חוֹצְצוֹת?
phrases.english: What, doesn't this mean that if they put them on, they do not block?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אמי's tradition from step 33.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אמי's rule that תפילין block.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Exempt' implies wearing them is allowed, and that is only possible if they do not block.

steps.title: No: even so, if worn they block
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the reading: the ברייתא does not mean the תפילין are harmless. If worn, they still block.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. If they put them on, the תפילין do block.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבי אמי. It says the word 'exempt' does not prove that תפילין don't block.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer refuses the inference from step 34. It keeps the rule that תפילין block. The word 'exempt' still needs explaining, and step 37 explains it.

phrases.english: No, if they put them on, they block.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference drawn in step 34.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejecting the inference from the wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Exempt' means a כהן may wear תפילין without harm.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even according to the ברייתא, תפילין worn by a כהן block.

steps.title: Then it should have said 'forbidden'
steps.stepSummary: If the תפילין block, the ברייתא should have said כהנים are 'forbidden' to wear them, not merely 'exempt'.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why does it say 'exempt'? It should have said 'forbidden'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from step 35. If wearing תפילין ruins the עבודה, the right word would be 'forbidden'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חציצה makes the service invalid, so wearing תפילין would be forbidden for a כהן. The soft word 'exempt' still seems to argue against רבי אמי.

phrases.english: If so, why does it say 'exempt'?!
It should have said 'forbidden'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 35 based on the ברייתא's wording.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 35 that the ברייתא agrees תפילין block.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If they block, the ברייתא should have said 'forbidden', not 'exempt'.

steps.title: 'Exempt' was chosen to fit לוים and ישראלים too
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא lists לוים and ישראלים as well, and they are not forbidden to wear תפילין. So it used one word, 'exempt', that fits everyone on the list.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the list also includes לוים and ישראלים, for whom 'forbidden' could not be taught, it taught 'exempt'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the word 'exempt'. The ברייתא chose a word that is true for all three groups.
steps.deeperAnalysis: לוים and ישראלים have no garment law, so they really are only exempt. For כהנים the deeper rule is 'forbidden', but the ברייתא used one shared word for the whole list. That keeps רבי אמי's rule standing.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't conclude that כהנים are only 'exempt'. For a כהן, wearing תפילין during the עבודה is really forbidden. The word 'exempt' was picked only to fit the whole list.

phrases.english: Since there are also Levites and Israelites in the list,
about whom it could not teach 'forbidden',
phrases.notes: לוים and ישראלים don't wear priestly garments, so there is nothing for תפילין to block.

phrases.english: because of this it taught 'exempt'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording challenge in step 36.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining why that word was chosen
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Exempt' shows that כהנים may wear תפילין.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Exempt' was used because it fits the לוים and ישראלים in the same list.

steps.title: Another ברייתא says outright: they do not block
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says clearly that if a כהן put on תפילין, they do not block.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught: if he put them on, they do not block!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now brings a direct contradiction to רבי אמי. A ברייתא openly says תפילין do not block.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time there is no word to reinterpret. This ברייתא states the opposite of רבי אמי's tradition, so the two teachings seem to clash head-on.

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught:
If he put them on, they do not block!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new and more direct challenge to רבי אמי, coming after step 37 settled the first one.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אמי's tradition that תפילין block.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא openly rules the opposite.

steps.title: Hand תפילין block; head תפילין do not
steps.stepSummary: The two teachings don't clash. The teaching that תפילין block is about the hand תפילין. The ברייתא that says they don't block is about the head תפילין.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult: this one is about hand תפילין, and that one is about head תפילין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction by splitting the cases. Hand תפילין block, and head תפילין do not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both teachings are kept by applying each one to a different kind of תפילין. רבי אמי's 'they block' refers to the hand תפילין. The ברייתא's 'they do not block' refers to the head תפילין.

keyTerms.meaning: Of the hand / of the head

steps.whatToRemember: Final picture: a כהן's hand תפילין count as a חציצה and ruin his עבודה. His head תפילין do not. The ברייתא's word 'exempt' was chosen only to cover לוים and ישראלים too.

phrases.english: It is not difficult;
this one is about the hand tefillin, that one is about the head tefillin.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא; הָא דְּיָד, הָא דְּרֹאשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the contradiction raised in step 38.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two teachings contradict each other about all תפילין.
steps.terutzMaskana: Hand תפילין block; head תפילין do not.

steps.title: Why are the hand תפילין different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why only the hand תפילין block. It suggests the reason is the פסוק 'ילבש על בשרו,' which teaches that nothing may come between the garment and the body.
steps.simpleTranslation: What makes the hand תפילין different? It is written, 'He shall put on upon his flesh,' which teaches that nothing may block between the garment and his flesh.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of Step 39's distinction. It suggests that a פסוק about the כהן's clothing explains why the hand תפילין block.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'על בשרו' ('on his flesh') mean the בגדי כהונה must touch the body directly. The hand תפילין sit under the sleeve, so they come between the garment and the arm. This step gives the reason for the hand, and it sets up the next question about the head.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? (asks why one case is treated differently from another)
He shall put on upon his flesh (ויקרא 6:3)

phrases.english: What is different about the hand [תפילין]?
As it is written: "He shall put on upon his flesh"
phrases.notes: ויקרא 6:3

phrases.english: that nothing should block
between it and his flesh;

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: קשיא (the question and the next line can be read together as one challenge)
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the scriptural basis of Step 39's split between hand and head תפילין.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why do only the hand תפילין count as a block?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק 'ילבש על בשרו' requires that nothing come between the garment and the body.

steps.title: The head has a similar פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reason it just gave. The פסוק about the מצנפת also says 'על ראשו,' so the head תפילין should block too.
steps.simpleTranslation: But about the head it is also written: 'And you shall place the turban upon his head'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the reason from Step 40. If 'on his flesh' makes the hand תפילין a block, then 'on his head' should make the head תפילין a block too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two פסוקים seem to work the same way: one says 'on his flesh' and the other says 'on his head.' If both mean nothing may come in between, then Step 39's split between hand and head falls apart. The גמרא now needs to show why the head is different.

keyTerms.meaning: The turban of the כהן גדול
And you shall place the turban upon his head (שמות 29:6)

phrases.english: About the head too, it is written:
"And you shall place the turban upon his head"!
phrases.notes: שמות 29:6

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in Step 40.
steps.kashyaTarget: The distinction between hand and head תפילין (Step 39), as explained in Step 40
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The head has a parallel פסוק, 'על ראשו.' By the same reasoning, the head תפילין should also block.

steps.title: The hair showed between the ציץ and the מצנפת
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts its answer with a ברייתא: the כהן גדול's hair was visible between the ציץ and the מצנפת. The full answer continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: His hair was visible between the ציץ and the turban.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins answering the challenge by quoting a ברייתא about how the כהן גדול wore the ציץ and the מצנפת. This line sets up the answer; the full explanation comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא shows that the ציץ and the מצנפת did not cover the head as one solid block, since a strip of hair showed between them. That open space is where the head תפילין would be placed. The גמרא will use this fact to show why the head תפילין do not count as a block.

keyTerms.meaning: The gold plate worn on the forehead of the כהן גדול

steps.confusionAlert: This is only the start of the answer. The גמרא has not yet said exactly how the visible hair solves the problem; that comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: It was taught:
His hair was visible
phrases.notes: He means the hair of the כהן גדול.

phrases.english: between the ציץ and the turban,

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא: שְׂעָרוֹ הָיָה נִרְאֶה בֵּין צִיץ לְמִצְנֶפֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering Step 41's challenge by describing how the head garments were placed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual setup from a ברייתא (the answer continues on the next amud)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The head garments cover the head completely, so the head תפילין would come between them and the head.
steps.terutzMaskana: There was an open space of hair between the ציץ and the מצנפת. The full answer follows on the next amud.
